A critic is a person who carefully studies, evaluates, and judges something — and then shares that judgment, usually in words. The key idea is that a critic does not just say "I liked it" or "I didn't like it." A critic explains why something is good or bad, using thought, knowledge, and reasoning.

Think of a critic as someone whose job — or strong habit — is to look at something closely, weigh its strengths and weaknesses, and deliver a verdict that others can learn from.
The Two Main Ways the Word Is Used

1. A Professional Critic

This is someone whose actual job is to evaluate works in a specific field and share opinions publicly — usually in newspapers, magazines, websites, or on television.

Some common types of professional critics:

  • A film critic watches movies and writes reviews telling audiences whether a film is worth watching and why.
  • A music critic listens to albums or concerts and judges the quality of the music, the performance, and the artistry.
  • A literary critic reads books and analyzes them — examining writing style, themes, characters, and meaning.
  • A food critic visits restaurants, tastes meals, and evaluates the quality of the food, service, and experience.
  • An art critic examines paintings, sculptures, and other artworks, and interprets their meaning, technique, and value.

What all these people share is that they are knowledgeable experts in their fields. A film critic has watched thousands of films. A food critic has an educated and trained sense of taste. Their opinions carry weight because of that expertise.

2. An Everyday Critic

In casual, everyday language, a critic can simply mean anyone who regularly finds fault with something or someone. You might hear someone say, "My boss is my biggest critic," meaning their boss frequently points out what they're doing wrong. In this sense, the word is used more loosely, without implying professional expertise.
What Makes Someone a Critic, Not Just an Opinion-Giver?

This is an important distinction. Everyone has opinions, but not everyone is a critic. Here's the difference:

  • A random person might say, "That movie was boring."
  • A critic says, "That movie was boring because the screenplay failed to develop the characters meaningfully, the pacing in the second act was too slow, and the dialogue felt unnatural — unlike the director's earlier work, which balanced tension and emotion far more effectively."

A critic supports their judgment with analysis and reasoning. They break something down into its parts, examine each part, and then form a conclusion. Their goal is not just to express a feeling, but to illuminate — to help others see and understand something more deeply.

This is one of the most common misunderstandings about this word. Many people assume a critic is someone who only finds problems and tears things apart. That is not accurate.

A critic can — and often does — praise something. A good critic is balanced. They recognize both what works and what doesn't. When a music critic reviews a brilliant album, they will celebrate its strengths just as confidently as they would point out weaknesses in a poor one.

However, it is true that in everyday conversation, calling someone "a critic" or "critical" often leans negative — suggesting they focus too much on flaws. So the tone of the word depends on the context in which it is used.

Why do critics exist? What is their role in society?

  • They act as guides — helping people decide what to read, watch, listen to, or eat.
  • They act as interpreters — explaining complex works of art so that others can understand and appreciate them better.
  • They act as standards-keepers — holding creators accountable for quality, pushing the arts and other fields to improve.
  • They contribute to public conversation — a thoughtful review of a book or film can spark important discussions about culture, society, and ideas.

There is a long-standing tension between critics and the people whose work they judge. Creators — writers, directors, chefs, musicians — sometimes feel that critics do not fully understand the difficulty of making something. Critics, on the other hand, argue that an outside, informed perspective is exactly what is needed for honest evaluation. Both sides have a point. This tension is part of what makes the role of the critic both fascinating and controversial.

A critic is a careful, knowledgeable evaluator who judges something — a film, a book, a meal, a performance, or even a person's actions — and explains that judgment clearly and thoughtfully. The word can refer to a formal professional or, more loosely, to anyone in the habit of pointing out faults. A true critic is neither purely positive nor purely negative — they are honest, informed, and always able to explain why they think what they think.
